title: Kin to the divine
hookLine: if we're kin to the divine, why think meanly of ourselves? (Discourses 1.3, 1.9)

cards: A letter arrives: the emperor has adopted you. Overnight you're family to the man who rules the world. If that happened, Epictetus jokes, no one could stand your pride.
Then he turns the joke around. His students had been taught something much bigger than that letter: that they were kin to God. So why, he asks, do they go around thinking so little of themselves?

teach.h: TWO THINGS MIXED: BODY AND REASON.
teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter three. For the Stoics, God is the reason running through the whole universe, and every human carries a share of it: our own reason. That's the kinship.
Epictetus says people are made of two things mixed together: a body, which they share with the animals, and reason and judgment, which they share with the gods. Many, he says, lean toward the first.
Then he gets specific, the way he does.
Some become like wolves, faithless and treacherous. Some like lions, wild and cruel. Most, he says, end up as foxes: small, sly, getting away with things.
None of that is what people are made for. Chapter nine pushes it further.
Ask Socrates where he's from, Epictetus says, and he wouldn't answer Athens. He'd say: from the world. If you're kin to the reason that runs everything, you belong to all of it, not just to one town.
Other traditions have their own way of saying something nearby. Genesis says, in the King James words, "So God created man in his own image."

Jews and Christians read that their own way, and the Stoic idea is its own thing, built on reason. But both refuse to let a person think of themselves as small stuff. Epictetus isn't flattering anyone.
Kinship is a standard, not a compliment.
If you're family, act like it: not by bragging about the family name, but by living the way the family lives, fair, clear-headed, and not easily frightened.

how: Stoic readers often recall Epictetus' kinship argument when they catch themselves acting from fear or pettiness, and some simply straighten their posture as a physical reminder.

o: a bond of friendship formed through shared work
kinship: your reason is a share of the world's reason
the family line you inherit from your parents

games.q: kin to the divine: tap the pairs.
p: small, sly, getting away with things
from the world, not just Athens

s: Epictetus says most people end up like foxes
wolves and lions too, but he warns that most of us become small and sly.
for the Stoics, kinship with God puts some people above others
every human shares it; it's a standard to live up to, not a rank.
Epictetus says Socrates would call himself simply an Athenian
he says Socrates would answer that he's from the world.

games.q: you're Epictetus. a student says: I'm just a body, an ordinary animal. what do you answer?
o: you're body and reason mixed, and the reason is kin to the gods.
you're pure spirit; the body doesn't matter.
games.why: he says we're made of both: a body shared with animals, and reason shared with the gods. most people lean toward the body.

practice: Let your spine come up tall, not stiff, the crown of your head lifting a little and the shoulders dropping as you breathe.

Then picture a place where you usually shrink, a meeting, a phone call, a relative's kitchen, and see yourself there, sitting this tall. Not proud, not loud: just someone who remembers what they're made of.

wordCard.voice: Syngeneia, the Greek word for kinship: our reason is a share of the reason that runs the world, so no one should think small of themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek syngeneia: kinship, being of one family; Epictetus uses it for our relation to God.

carryVoice: Your line: kin. Not small stuff, and not a fox, but family to reason itself. See you tomorrow.
